title: Pole Positions and the Time Signal
intro: Where a pole sits tells you what the signal does: how far left it lies sets how fast the signal decays or grows, and how far up it lies sets how fast it oscillates. Stability is the question of which side of the imaginary axis the poles are on.

blocks.text: One pole, one exponential

A single pole at $p$ with a right-sided region is the signal $e^{pt}u(t)$: its transform is $1/(s - p)$. With a real pole $p = -a$ that is $e^{-at}u(t)$, and the position of the pole is the whole story:

items: Left of the imaginary axis ($a > 0$): the signal decays. The farther left, the faster. The time constant is $1/a$: for $a = 0.5$ it is 2 s, and the signal is $e^{-1} = 0.368$ of its start at $t = 2$, $0.135$ at $t = 4$ and $0.050$ at $t = 6$. It is below 1% of the start after $\ln(100)/0.5 = 9.2$ s.
On the axis ($a = 0$): neither growth nor decay. The pole at 0 is the unit step.
Right of the axis ($a < 0$): the signal grows. With $a = -0.2$ it multiplies by $e^{2} = 7.39$ every 10 s and doubles every $\ln 2/0.2 = 3.47$ s.

blocks.text: This is the continuous-time cousin of Pole Positions and the Time Signal (#/math/z-transform/poles-and-time): there the circle $|z| = 1$ was the border between decay and growth; here it is the imaginary axis, and a pole's distance from the origin is replaced by its horizontal position.
A pair of poles: a damped oscillation
A conjugate pair $p = -a \pm j\omega_0$ gives a damped sinusoid. Each pole contributes $e^{pt} = e^{-at}e^{\pm j\omega_0 t}$, and the two add into a real signal:

items: The height $\omega_0$ of the pole above the real axis is the oscillation frequency in radians per second: one oscillation takes $2\pi/\omega_0$ seconds.
The distance $a$ to the left is the decay rate: the envelope is $e^{-at}$.
Poles nearer the imaginary axis mean slower decay, a longer ring, and a sharper peak in the frequency response at $\omega \approx \omega_0$. A pair on the axis rings forever.

blocks.text: With $a = 0.5$ and $\omega_0 = 1.5$ the oscillation has a period of $2\pi/1.5 = 4.19$ s, and the envelope falls to $1/e$ in 2 s, so it completes only half a swing in that time: $2/4.19 = 0.48$ of a cycle. The signal is $e^{-0.5t}\sin(1.5t)$: its first peak is at $t = \arctan(1.5/0.5)/1.5 = 0.833$ s with value $0.626$, and at $t = 1$ s it is $0.605$ and at $t = 2$ s only $0.052$.

Watch the signal panel (top left) and the poles in the s-plane panel together. Drag Decay rate a from 0.5 down to 0: the poles slide right to the axis and the signal stops decaying. Push a negative, to $-0.2$ for example: the poles are right of the axis, the signal grows, and the viewer's last step says the system is unstable (and that the Fourier transform does not exist, since the region is $\operatorname{Re} s > 0.2$). Now drag Frequency ω₀ from 1.5 to 2.5: the poles move up and the oscillation speeds up, from a period of $4.19$ s to $2.51$ s, while the envelope stays put.
Natural frequency and damping ratio
Engineers describe the same pair with two other numbers. A second-order denominator is written

The natural frequency $\omega_n$ is the distance of the poles from the origin, $|p| = \omega_n$. The damping ratio $\zeta$ is the cosine of the angle between the pole and the negative real axis, which is the decay rate over $\omega_n$. For the poles $-0.5 \pm j1.5$: $\omega_n = \sqrt{0.25 + 2.25} = 1.581$ rad/s and $\zeta = 0.5/1.581 = 0.316$; the angle is $71.6^\circ$, and $\cos 71.6^\circ = 0.316$. In the form above, $2\zeta\omega_n = 1.00$ and $\omega_n^2 = 2.5$, matching $s^2 + s + 2.5$.
Fix $\omega_n = 1$ and slide the poles round the circle of radius 1, from the imaginary axis to the negative real axis:

items: $\zeta = 0.1$: poles at $-0.1 \pm j0.995$. Nearly on the axis: a long ring.
$\zeta = 1$: a double pole at $-1$. This is critical damping, the fastest return to rest without oscillation.
$\zeta = 2$: two real poles, at $-0.268$ and $-3.73$. Overdamped, with two separate exponentials, a slow one and a fast one. The slow pole decides how long the signal lasts.

blocks.text: For a step input, a second-order system overshoots its final value by $e^{-\pi\zeta/\sqrt{1-\zeta^2}}$; with $\zeta = 0.316$ that is $35.1\%$. The page Solving Differential Equations (#/math/laplace-transform/differential-equations) gets the same number from a mass on a spring.
Repeated poles
Two poles at the same place give a factor $t$:

The signal rises first, as $t$ wins, and then decays, as the exponential wins. It peaks at $t = 1/a$ with value $1/(ae)$; for $a = 0.5$ that is $t = 2$ s and $0.736$. A double pole on the imaginary axis, $t\,u(t)$, is a ramp that grows without limit even though $1^t$ does not: repeated poles on the axis are unstable. In the viewer pick ramped exponential and the s-plane panel marks the pole with $\times 2$.

The signal panel shows the rise to a peak near $t = 2$ s and then the decay. Drag Decay rate a to 1: the peak moves to $t = 1$ s and the double pole is at $-1$; drag it to 0.1 and the peak slides out beyond 8 s, off the right of the panel, while the pole creeps toward the axis. Compare the surface with the single pole of decaying exponential: the double pole rises twice as steeply in decibels.
Stability

A causal system is BIBO stable exactly when every pole of its transfer function lies strictly in the left half-plane. The reason is on the page The Region of Convergence (#/math/laplace-transform/region-of-convergence): causal means the region is to the right of the rightmost pole, stable means the imaginary axis is in the region, and both hold only if the rightmost pole is left of the axis. A simple pole on the axis (a step, a steady sine) gives a signal that never dies out; a double pole there, or a pole to the right, gives one that grows.

Sampling a continuous signal every $T$ seconds maps the s-plane to the z-plane by $z = e^{sT}$: the left half-plane lands inside the unit circle, and the imaginary axis is wrapped around the circle. The page A Gallery of Signals (#/math/laplace-transform/gallery) makes this precise with numbers.
Problems

blocks.title: Read a pole plot
blocks.text: A causal signal has poles at $-2 \pm j3$ and nothing else. Describe it.
solution: The decay rate is $2$ per second, so the envelope is $e^{-2t}$, with time constant $0.5$ s. The oscillation has $\omega_0 = 3$ rad/s, a period of $2\pi/3 = 2.09$ s. So about four time constants pass in one period: it is heavily damped, and after one swing it is gone ($e^{-2 \times 2.09} = 0.015$). The natural frequency is $\sqrt{4 + 9} = 3.61$ rad/s and $\zeta = 2/3.61 = 0.555$. Both poles are left of the axis: stable.

blocks.title: Find the poles
blocks.text: A system has $\omega_n = 4$ rad/s and $\zeta = 0.2$. Where are its poles, and how long does it take for the envelope to fall to $1/e$?
solution: $-\zeta\omega_n = -0.8$ and $\omega_n\sqrt{1 - \zeta^2} = 4 \times 0.9798 = 3.919$. So the poles are at $-0.8 \pm j3.92$, and the envelope $e^{-0.8t}$ falls to $1/e$ after $1/0.8 = 1.25$ s.

blocks.title: Unstable or not?
blocks.text: Which causal transfer functions are stable? (a) $1/(s - 0.1)$; (b) $1/(s + 0.5)$; (c) $1/s^2$; (d) $1/(s^2 + 4)$.
solution: (a) pole at $+0.1$, right of the axis: unstable, $e^{0.1t}$. (b) pole at $-0.5$: stable. (c) double pole at 0: the ramp $t\,u(t)$, unstable. (d) poles at $\pm j2$ on the axis: $\tfrac12\sin 2t$, which never grows or decays, and is not BIBO stable (a bounded input at 2 rad/s makes the output grow without limit).
